L0|easy.title: Gravitational PE to KE: Ball Drop Energy
L0|easy.statement:
A steel ball bearing of mass $m = 0.25\,\text{kg}$ is dropped from a height of $h = 5.0\,\text{m}$ above a rigid floor in a closed, thermally insulated chamber. Assume the ball starts from rest and that no air resistance acts on it during the fall.

(a) Calculate the gravitational potential energy (PE) stored in the ball at the start.

(b) Calculate the kinetic energy (KE) of the ball just before it strikes the floor.

(c) State which form(s) of kinetic energy — translational, rotational, or vibrational — describe the ball's motion during the fall.

Use $g = 9.81\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2}$.
L0|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Gravitational Potential Energy

The gravitational PE stored in the ball at height $h$ relative to the floor is:

$$\text{PE} = mgh$$

Substituting the given values:

$$\text{PE} = 0.25\,\text{kg} \times 9.81\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2} \times 5.0\,\text{m}$$

$$\boxed{\text{PE} = 12.3\,\text{J}}$$

## Step 2 — Kinetic Energy Just Before Impact

By the First Law of Thermodynamics (energy conservation), the system is thermally insulated and no work is done by friction. All of the initial PE converts to KE by the time the ball reaches the floor:

$$\Delta \text{PE} + \Delta \text{KE} = 0$$

Since the ball starts from rest ($\text{KE}_\text{initial} = 0$) and the floor is the reference level ($\text{PE}_\text{final} = 0$):

$$\text{KE}_\text{final} = \text{PE}_\text{initial} = mgh$$

$$\text{KE} = 0.25 \times 9.81 \times 5.0$$

$$\boxed{\text{KE} = 12.3\,\text{J}}$$

We can verify this using $\text{KE} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. The velocity just before impact is:

$$v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 5.0} = \sqrt{98.1} \approx 9.90\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$$

$$\text{KE} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.25 \times (9.90)^2 = 0.125 \times 98.0 \approx 12.3\,\text{J} \checkmark$$

## Step 3 — Type of Kinetic Energy

The ball as a whole moves downward in a straight line — this is **translational** kinetic energy. The centre of mass of the ball translates through space; neither rotation about an axis nor internal atomic vibrations (which would constitute thermal energy) are involved in describing the macroscopic motion of the ball during free fall.
common_mistakes: Confusing gravitational PE ($mgh$) with kinetic energy ($\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$) — students sometimes try to set $mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ but then forget this only works because energy is conserved (no friction), and so treat it as always valid even when dissipation is present.
Calling the ball's downward motion 'vibrational' or 'rotational' — these terms refer to internal molecular modes or spinning about an axis, not straight-line translation of the centre of mass.
Using $g = 10\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2}$ without justification, giving $\text{PE} = 12.5\,\text{J}$ instead of $12.3\,\text{J}$ — always use the value specified in the problem.

L0|easy.title: Work Done Lifting a Steel Ingot
L0|easy.statement:
A robotic arm in a steel foundry lifts a solid steel ingot of mass $m = 12\,\text{kg}$ vertically upward through a height of $h = 3.5\,\text{m}$ at constant velocity.

(a) How much work does the robotic arm do on the ingot?

(b) By how much does the gravitational potential energy of the ingot change?

(c) State whether the ingot's kinetic energy changes during the lift, and explain why.

Use $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$.
L0|easy.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Work done by the robotic arm

Work is defined as force acting through a displacement. To lift the ingot at **constant velocity**, the arm must apply a force exactly equal to the weight of the ingot (no net acceleration):

$$F = mg = 12 \times 9.81 = 117.72\,\text{N}$$

The displacement is parallel to the applied force (both upward), so:

$$W = F \cdot d = mg \times h = 117.72 \times 3.5$$

$$\boxed{W = 412.0\,\text{J}}$$

### Part (b) — Change in gravitational potential energy

Gravitational potential energy is given by:

$$\text{PE} = mgh$$

The change in PE from initial to final position is:

$$\Delta \text{PE} = mg\Delta h = 12 \times 9.81 \times 3.5$$

$$\boxed{\Delta \text{PE} = 412.0\,\text{J}}$$

This confirms that **all the work done by the arm went into gravitational PE** of the ingot — consistent with energy conservation (First Law).

### Part (c) — Change in kinetic energy

The ingot is lifted at **constant velocity**, meaning $\Delta v = 0$. Since $\text{KE} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, and $v$ does not change:

$$\Delta \text{KE} = \tfrac{1}{2}m(v_f^2 - v_i^2) = \tfrac{1}{2}m(0) = 0$$

The kinetic energy does **not change**. The robotic arm's work goes entirely into raising the gravitational PE, with zero going into translational KE. This is a direct consequence of Newton's second law: constant velocity implies zero net force, so the applied force exactly balances gravity at every instant.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that constant velocity means the applied force equals weight exactly — students sometimes try to add an extra 'lifting force' on top of $mg$, double-counting the force.

Confusing work done by the arm with the net work done on the ingot. The net work on the ingot is zero (since $\Delta\text{KE} = 0$); the arm's work equals the gain in PE, which is balanced by gravity doing negative work on the ingot.
Using mass in grams rather than kilograms in the formula $W = mgh$, leading to an answer 1000 times too small when SI units (joules) are expected.

L0|easy.title: Gravitational PE to KE Conversion for a Falling Sample
L0|easy.statement:
A small ceramic sample of mass $m = 0.25\,\text{kg}$ is accidentally knocked off a laboratory shelf that is $h = 1.6\,\text{m}$ above the floor. Assuming all of its gravitational potential energy converts to kinetic energy just before it hits the ground, and that $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$:

(a) Calculate the gravitational potential energy (PE) stored in the sample while it sits on the shelf (relative to the floor).

(b) State what the kinetic energy (KE) of the sample is just before impact.

(c) Using the result from (b), calculate the speed $v$ of the sample just before it hits the floor.
L0|easy.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Gravitational PE

The gravitational potential energy stored in an object held at height $h$ above a reference level is:

$$\text{PE} = mgh$$

Substituting the given values:

$$\text{PE} = 0.25\,\text{kg} \times 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2 \times 1.6\,\text{m}$$

$$\boxed{\text{PE} = 3.924\,\text{J}}$$

---

### Part (b) — KE just before impact

By conservation of energy (First Law reasoning: energy is never created or destroyed), all the gravitational PE converts to translational kinetic energy as the sample falls, assuming no energy is lost to air resistance:

$$\text{KE} = \text{PE} = \boxed{3.924\,\text{J}}$$

---

### Part (c) — Speed just before impact

The kinetic energy of a mass moving at speed $v$ is:

$$\text{KE} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$

Rearranging for $v$:

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{2\,\text{KE}}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 3.924\,\text{J}}{0.25\,\text{kg}}}$$

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{7.848}{0.25}} = \sqrt{31.39}$$

$$\boxed{v \approx 5.60\,\text{m/s}}$$

---

### Sanity check

Alternatively, using kinematics: $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 1.6} = \sqrt{31.39} \approx 5.60\,\text{m/s}$ ✓

The two routes agree, confirming energy conservation is correctly applied.
common_mistakes: **Forgetting to square-root at the end.** Students often write $v = 2\,\text{KE}/m$ without taking the square root, getting $v = 31.4\,\text{m/s}$ — a factor of $\sqrt{31.4}$ too large.

**Using mass in grams instead of kilograms.** If $m = 250\,\text{g}$ is used without converting, the PE and speed will be off by factors of $\sqrt{1000}$; the unit of energy (J = kg·m²/s²) requires SI units throughout.

**Confusing PE and KE as additive rather than interconverting.** Some students add PE and KE at the bottom of the fall, writing $\text{KE} = mgh + \frac{1}{2}mv^2$, double-counting the energy rather than recognising that PE has fully converted into KE.

L0|easy.title: Gravitational PE to KE Conversion on a Ski Slope
L0|easy.statement:
A skier of mass 70 kg descends a frictionless ski slope, dropping a vertical height of 15 m. Assume the skier starts from rest and that the slope is perfectly insulated so no heat is transferred to or from the skier.

(a) Calculate the gravitational potential energy (PE) lost by the skier over this descent.

(b) If all of this lost PE is converted to kinetic energy (KE), calculate the speed of the skier at the bottom of the slope.

Use $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
L0|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — State the energy principle

For an isolated system (no heat transfer, no friction), the First Law of Thermodynamics and energy conservation together require that the total mechanical energy is constant:

$$\Delta U = Q + W = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{PE lost} = \text{KE gained}$$

Since $Q = 0$ (insulated, no heat transfer) and no non-conservative work is done (frictionless), all potential energy converts to kinetic energy.

## Part (a) — Gravitational PE lost

The gravitational potential energy is:
$$\text{PE} = mgh$$

Substituting values:
$$\text{PE} = 70\ \mathrm{kg} \times 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} \times 15\ \mathrm{m}$$

$$\boxed{\text{PE} = 10{,}290\ \mathrm{J} \approx 10.3\ \mathrm{kJ}}$$

## Part (b) — Speed at the bottom

Setting PE lost equal to KE gained:
$$mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$$

The mass cancels:
$$gh = \tfrac{1}{2}v^2$$

Solving for $v$:
$$v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} \times 15\ \mathrm{m}}$$

$$v = \sqrt{294.3}$$

$$\boxed{v \approx 17.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}}$$

## Sanity check

- KE at bottom: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 70 \times (17.2)^2 = 35 \times 295.8 \approx 10{,}353\ \mathrm{J}$ — consistent with PE lost (small rounding difference). ✓
- Units: $\mathrm{kg \cdot m^2 \cdot s^{-2}} = \mathrm{J}$ ✓
- The speed of ~17 m/s (~62 km/h) is physically plausible for a frictionless 15 m vertical drop on a ski slope. ✓
common_mistakes: Forgetting that the mass cancels in the energy balance $mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, and attempting to use the PE formula alone to find speed without forming the equation correctly.
Confusing the vertical height drop $h$ with the length of the slope along the surface — only the vertical component $h$ enters $\text{PE} = mgh$.

Not recognising that the 'system' here must be defined carefully: the skier is the system, gravitational PE is the form of internal stored energy being converted, and the frictionless/insulated conditions mean $Q = 0$ and $W_{\text{non-conservative}} = 0$, making the conversion exact.

L0|easy.title: Classifying Properties of a Gas Sample
L0|easy.statement:
A rigid, sealed container holds a fixed amount of nitrogen gas. A student records the following properties of the gas at equilibrium:

| Property | Symbol | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Temperature | $T$ | 350 K |
| Pressure | $P$ | 2.5 atm |
| Total volume | $V$ | 0.020 m³ |
| Total internal energy | $U$ | 4800 J |
| Amount | $n$ | 1.74 mol |
| Mass | $m$ | 48.7 g |

For **each** of the six properties listed above, state whether it is:

(a) **Intensive** or **Extensive**, and

(b) A **state function** or a **path function**.

Then compute the **specific internal energy** $\underline{U} = U/m$ in J/kg and classify the result as intensive or extensive.
L0|easy.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) and (b) — Classify each property

Recall the definitions from L0:
- **Extensive** property: scales with the amount (size) of the system. If you double the system, the property doubles.
- **Intensive** property: independent of the amount. Doubling the system leaves the value unchanged.
- **State function**: depends only on the current macrostate, not on the history or path taken. Examples: $T$, $P$, $V$, $U$.
- **Path function**: depends on the process (path) by which the system changed. Examples: heat $Q$, work $W$.

| Property | Intensive or Extensive? | State or Path function? | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|---|
| $T = 350$ K | **Intensive** | **State function** | Temperature does not double if you combine two identical boxes of gas. Determined entirely by current macrostate. |
| $P = 2.5$ atm | **Intensive** | **State function** | Pressure is the same throughout the gas at equilibrium; independent of amount. |
| $V = 0.020$ m³ | **Extensive** | **State function** | Doubling the gas doubles the total volume. Value fixed by current macrostate. |
| $U = 4800$ J | **Extensive** | **State function** | Total internal energy scales with amount of gas. Fixed by macrostate (not by path). |
| $n = 1.74$ mol | **Extensive** | **State function** | Amount of substance scales with system size. |
| $m = 48.7$ g | **Extensive** | **State function** | Mass scales with system size. |

> **Key point:** All six properties listed are **state functions**. Heat $Q$ and work $W$ are the path functions you will encounter — they are *not* properties of a state, because they depend on how the system got there. None of the listed quantities are path functions.

---

### Part (c) — Compute specific internal energy

The specific internal energy is defined as the internal energy per unit mass:

$$\underline{U} = \frac{U}{m}$$

Convert mass to kg:

$$m = 48.7 \text{ g} = 0.0487 \text{ kg}$$

Substitute:

$$\underline{U} = \frac{4800 \text{ J}}{0.0487 \text{ kg}} \approx \boxed{98{,}562 \text{ J/kg} \approx 98.6 \text{ kJ/kg}}$$

**Classification of $\underline{U}$:**

$\underline{U}$ is the **ratio of two extensive properties** ($U$ and $m$). By the rule from L0 — *the ratio of two extensive properties is intensive* — specific internal energy is **intensive**.

Sanity check: if you doubled the system (doubled both $U$ and $m$), the ratio $U/m$ would be unchanged. ✓
L0|easy.final_answer: $\underline{U} = U/m = 4800\,\text{J} / 0.0487\,\text{kg} \approx 98{,}600\,\text{J/kg}$ (intensive). All six listed properties are state functions; $T$ and $P$ are intensive; $V$, $U$, $n$, $m$ are extensive.
common_mistakes: Classifying heat $Q$ or work $W$ as state functions. Students often conflate 'property of the gas' with 'state function'. $Q$ and $W$ are path functions — but none of the six quantities listed in this problem are $Q$ or $W$, so all six are state functions.

Calling temperature or pressure 'extensive' because they have units or are measurable. Intensive vs. extensive is about scaling with system size, not about having units. $T$ and $P$ stay the same if you double the system.

Thinking that specific internal energy $\underline{U} = U/m$ is still extensive because $U$ by itself is extensive. The division by $m$ (also extensive) makes the ratio intensive — a key general rule: ratio of two extensives = intensive.

L0|easy.title: Gravitational PE to KE: Falling Steel Ball
L0|easy.statement:
A steel ball bearing of mass $m = 0.080\,\text{kg}$ is dropped from rest from a height of $h = 5.0\,\text{m}$ above a hard floor in a vacuum (no air resistance). Using $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$:

(a) Calculate the gravitational potential energy (PE) stored in the ball at the initial height.

(b) What is the kinetic energy (KE) of the ball just before it hits the floor?

(c) State which type of kinetic energy (translational, rotational, or vibrational) the ball possesses just before impact, and classify the ball's motion as an example of which form of macroscopic energy storage.
L0|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Gravitational Potential Energy

The gravitational PE of an object of mass $m$ at height $h$ above a reference level is:

$$\text{PE} = mgh$$

Substituting the given values:

$$\text{PE} = (0.080\,\text{kg})(9.81\,\text{m/s}^2)(5.0\,\text{m})$$

$$\boxed{\text{PE} = 3.924\,\text{J} \approx 3.92\,\text{J}}$$

## Step 2 — Kinetic Energy Just Before Impact

By conservation of energy (the system is in a vacuum — no friction or air resistance), all the initial PE converts to KE as the ball falls:

$$\Delta \text{PE} + \Delta \text{KE} = 0$$

$$\text{KE}_{\text{final}} = \text{PE}_{\text{initial}} - \text{PE}_{\text{final}}$$

Taking the floor as the reference level, $\text{PE}_{\text{final}} = 0$, so:

$$\text{KE} = \text{PE} = mgh = 3.92\,\text{J}$$

$$\boxed{\text{KE} = 3.92\,\text{J}}$$

As a check, the impact speed can be computed:

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{2\,\text{KE}}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 3.924}{0.080}} = \sqrt{98.1} \approx 9.90\,\text{m/s}$$

Alternatively, $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 5.0} = \sqrt{98.1} \approx 9.90\,\text{m/s}$ ✓

## Step 3 — Classification of KE and Energy Form

The ball moves as a single rigid body in a straight line downward — its centre of mass is translating through space. Therefore the KE is **translational kinetic energy**.

This is a **macroscopic** (bulk) form of energy storage — the entire object is moving coherently, not individual molecules vibrating internally. The First Law of Thermodynamics distinguishes macroscopic KE (like this) from **internal energy** $U$, which captures the microscopic kinetic energy of individual atoms/molecules. As long as the ball remains rigid and un-deformed, all of its kinetic energy is macroscopic translational KE — none has been converted to internal energy (heat).
L0|easy.final_answer: (a) $\text{PE} = 3.92\,\text{J}$; (b) $\text{KE} = 3.92\,\text{J}$; (c) Translational kinetic energy — a macroscopic (bulk) form of energy storage.
common_mistakes: Confusing gravitational PE with internal energy $U$. Gravitational PE is a macroscopic potential energy stored by virtue of the object's position in a gravitational field; $U$ is the sum of microscopic molecular kinetic and potential energies. They are distinct quantities in the First Law framework.

Setting $\text{KE} \neq \text{PE}$ by forgetting that vacuum conditions mean no energy is lost to drag or friction. Students sometimes try to subtract an air-resistance work term that is not present here.

Classifying the ball's motion as rotational or vibrational KE. The ball translates as a whole along a straight path; rotational KE would require spinning, and vibrational KE refers to atomic-scale oscillations — neither applies to a freely falling rigid sphere in this problem.

L0|easy.title: Classifying System Boundaries in a Pressure Cooker
L0|easy.statement:
A sealed pressure cooker sits on a stovetop. The cooker is made of thick stainless steel and has a pressure-relief valve that remains closed throughout the cooking process. Steam builds up inside as the food cooks.

(a) Identify whether the pressure cooker (as the system) is best described as **open**, **closed**, or **isolated**. Justify your answer by stating which of the following can cross the boundary: matter, heat, and work.

(b) The stainless steel walls of the cooker conduct heat from the flame at a rate that delivers $Q = +8{,}500$ J to the system over 5 minutes. The steam inside pushes outward on the rigid walls but the walls do not move, so no boundary displacement occurs. Using the sign convention $\Delta U = Q + W$, calculate the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ of the cooker contents over those 5 minutes.

*Note:* Surface tension, electrical, and magnetic work are negligible. The pressure-relief valve stays closed, so no mass escapes.
L0|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Classify the system type

Ask three questions about the boundary:

| Quantity | Crosses the boundary? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Matter** | No | The valve is closed; the lid is sealed. No steam escapes and no food enters. |
| **Heat** | Yes | The steel walls are thermally conductive; the flame heats the contents. |
| **Work** | No net $PV$ work | The walls are **rigid** — no volume change, so $\delta W = -P\,\mathrm{d}V = 0$. |

Because matter cannot cross the boundary but energy (heat) can, the pressure cooker is a **closed system**.

---

## Step 2 — Identify $Q$ and $W$

Using the course convention (L0 §0.7):
$$\Delta U = Q + W$$

- **Heat:** $Q = +8{,}500\;\text{J}$ (heat is absorbed *by* the system, so positive by convention).
- **Work:** The walls are rigid, so $\mathrm{d}V = 0$ throughout. Therefore:
$$W = -P\,\Delta V = -P \times 0 = 0\;\text{J}$$

---

## Step 3 — Apply the First Law

$$\Delta U = Q + W = 8{,}500 + 0 = \boxed{+8{,}500\;\text{J}}$$

---

## Step 4 — Physical interpretation

All of the heat delivered by the flame goes directly into raising the **internal energy** of the cooker contents (raising $T$ and $P$ of the steam and food). No energy is lost as $PV$ work because the rigid walls prevent any expansion. This is why pressure cookers reach higher temperatures than open pots — no energy 'leaks out' as expansion work against the atmosphere.
common_mistakes: Treating the pressure cooker as an **isolated** system because 'it is sealed'. Sealed means no matter crosses, but heat still crosses the conductive steel walls — so it is closed, not isolated. Isolation requires *both* matter *and* energy to be blocked.

Assigning $W = -P\Delta V$ a non-zero value because there is pressure inside the cooker. Students sometimes multiply the internal gauge pressure by the vessel volume. But $W = -P\,\Delta V$ depends on whether the *volume changes*, not on whether pressure exists — rigid walls mean $\Delta V = 0$ and therefore $W = 0$.

Using the wrong sign for $Q$, writing $Q = -8{,}500$ J because 'heat comes from outside'. Under the MS1016 convention, $Q > 0$ when heat flows *into* the system. The flame is outside; the system absorbs the heat, so $Q$ is positive.

L0|easy.title: Classifying Thermodynamic Properties: Specific Heat Capacity vs. Total Heat Capacity
L0|easy.statement:
A student measures the heat capacity of a 3.0 kg block of aluminium (Al) and finds that the total heat capacity of the block is $C_\text{total} = 2709\text{ J/K}$. The atomic weight of aluminium is 27 g/mol.

(a) Is the total heat capacity $C_\text{total}$ an intensive or an extensive property? Justify your answer in one sentence.

(b) Calculate the **molar heat capacity** $\underline{C}$ (per mole) of aluminium from the data given.

(c) Is the molar heat capacity intensive or extensive? Justify your answer.
L0|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Answer part (a): Is $C_\text{total}$ intensive or extensive?

An **extensive** property scales with the amount of material. If we doubled the mass of the aluminium block from 3.0 kg to 6.0 kg, the total heat capacity would double to 5418 J/K. Therefore $C_\text{total}$ is **extensive**.

## Step 2 — Convert mass to moles

The molar mass of Al is 27 g/mol = 0.027 kg/mol.

$$n = \frac{m}{M} = \frac{3.0\text{ kg}}{0.027\text{ kg/mol}} = 111.1\text{ mol}$$

## Step 3 — Calculate the molar heat capacity

The molar heat capacity is the total heat capacity divided by the number of moles:

$$\underline{C} = \frac{C_\text{total}}{n} = \frac{2709\text{ J/K}}{111.1\text{ mol}} = 24.4\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

## Step 4 — Answer part (c): Is $\underline{C}$ intensive or extensive?

The molar heat capacity is the **ratio of two extensive quantities** ($C_\text{total}$ and $n$). Any ratio of two extensive properties is **intensive** — it does not depend on how much material is present. Whether you have 1 kg or 100 kg of aluminium, the molar heat capacity remains 24.4 J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.

**Final Answers:**
- (a) Extensive
- (b) $\underline{C} = 24.4\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$
- (c) Intensive
common_mistakes: Confusing extensive and intensive: students often say heat capacity is intensive because it is a material property, but the *total* heat capacity of a specific object is extensive — it doubles when you double the mass.
Dividing by mass in kg instead of number of moles, yielding a specific heat in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ rather than the requested molar heat capacity in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Forgetting to convert the molar mass from g/mol to kg/mol before dividing into the mass in kg, leading to an answer 1000 times too small.

L0|easy.title: Identifying Intensive vs. Extensive Properties of a Gas Sample
L0|easy.statement:
A sealed container holds 3 moles of an ideal gas at a temperature of 350 K, a pressure of 2.5 atm, and a total volume of 34.4 L. The total internal energy of the gas is $U = 13{,}050$ J, and the total mass of gas is 96 g.

For each of the following properties, classify it as either **intensive** or **extensive**, and justify your answer by checking whether the property changes if you consider only half the gas sample (1.5 mol) in half the volume at the same temperature and pressure:

1. Temperature $T = 350$ K
2. Total volume $V = 34.4$ L
3. Pressure $P = 2.5$ atm
4. Total internal energy $U = 13{,}050$ J
5. Molar internal energy $\underline{U} = U/n$
6. Density $\rho = m/V$
L0|easy.solution:
## Strategy

An **extensive** property scales with the amount of matter — doubling the system doubles the property. An **intensive** property does not depend on the amount of matter.

The test: consider exactly half the gas (1.5 mol, half the volume, same $T$ and $P$). Check whether each property changes.

---

### Half-system reference values

$$n_{\text{half}} = 1.5\;\text{mol}, \quad V_{\text{half}} = \frac{34.4}{2} = 17.2\;\text{L}, \quad m_{\text{half}} = \frac{96}{2} = 48\;\text{g}$$

$$U_{\text{half}} = \frac{13{,}050}{2} = 6{,}525\;\text{J}, \quad T_{\text{half}} = 350\;\text{K}, \quad P_{\text{half}} = 2.5\;\text{atm}$$

---

### Property-by-property classification

**1. Temperature $T = 350$ K**

The half-system is still at $T = 350$ K — temperature does not scale with amount.

$$\boxed{T \text{ is } \textbf{intensive}}$$

**2. Total volume $V = 34.4$ L**

The half-system occupies $V_{\text{half}} = 17.2$ L — exactly half. Volume scales with amount.

$$\boxed{V \text{ is } \textbf{extensive}}$$

**3. Pressure $P = 2.5$ atm**

The half-system is still at $P = 2.5$ atm — pressure does not scale with amount.

$$\boxed{P \text{ is } \textbf{intensive}}$$

**4. Total internal energy $U = 13{,}050$ J**

The half-system has $U_{\text{half}} = 6{,}525$ J — exactly half. Internal energy scales with amount.

$$\boxed{U \text{ is } \textbf{extensive}}$$

**5. Molar internal energy $\underline{U} = U/n$**

For the full system:
$$\underline{U} = \frac{13{,}050\;\text{J}}{3\;\text{mol}} = 4{,}350\;\text{J/mol}$$

For the half-system:
$$\underline{U}_{\text{half}} = \frac{6{,}525\;\text{J}}{1.5\;\text{mol}} = 4{,}350\;\text{J/mol}$$

Unchanged — as expected, since dividing two extensive quantities gives an intensive quantity.

$$\boxed{\underline{U} = U/n \text{ is } \textbf{intensive}}$$

**6. Density $\rho = m/V$**

For the full system:
$$\rho = \frac{96\;\text{g}}{34.4\;\text{L}} = 2.79\;\text{g/L}$$

For the half-system:
$$\rho_{\text{half}} = \frac{48\;\text{g}}{17.2\;\text{L}} = 2.79\;\text{g/L}$$

Unchanged — density is the ratio of two extensive properties (mass and volume), so it is intensive.

$$\boxed{\rho \text{ is } \textbf{intensive}}$$

---

### Summary table

| Property | Value (full) | Value (half) | Classification |
|---|---|---|---|
| $T$ | 350 K | 350 K | **Intensive** |
| $V$ | 34.4 L | 17.2 L | **Extensive** |
| $P$ | 2.5 atm | 2.5 atm | **Intensive** |
| $U$ | 13,050 J | 6,525 J | **Extensive** |
| $\underline{U} = U/n$ | 4,350 J/mol | 4,350 J/mol | **Intensive** |
| $\rho = m/V$ | 2.79 g/L | 2.79 g/L | **Intensive** |
common_mistakes: Classifying internal energy $U$ as intensive because it is an energy quantity — energy per se is not what determines intensive vs. extensive; the key test is whether it scales with system size. Since halving the gas halves $U$, it is extensive.

Classifying molar internal energy $\underline{U} = U/n$ as extensive because $U$ is extensive — the division by $n$ (also extensive) removes the size dependence, making the ratio intensive. The general rule is: ratio of two extensive quantities is intensive.

Confusing pressure with volume: students sometimes label pressure as extensive because 'a bigger container has more pressure', but pressure (force per unit area) is the same throughout a system at equilibrium regardless of size, making it intensive.

L0|easy.title: Classifying Energy Forms in a Spinning Flywheel
L0|easy.statement:
A solid steel flywheel of mass $m = 12\text{ kg}$ spins at an angular velocity of $\omega = 250\text{ rad/s}$ about its central axis. The moment of inertia of the flywheel about its axis is $I = 0.18\text{ kg·m}^2$.

(a) State whether the kinetic energy of the spinning flywheel is best classified as **translational**, **rotational**, or **vibrational** kinetic energy, and explain why.

(b) Calculate the rotational kinetic energy stored in the flywheel in joules.

(c) The flywheel is brought to rest by a friction brake. The brake converts all the rotational kinetic energy into **internal energy** (random molecular motion) of the flywheel material. If the specific heat capacity of steel is $c = 500\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$, estimate by how many kelvins the flywheel's temperature rises, assuming no heat is lost to the surroundings during braking.
L0|easy.solution:
## Step 1 — Classify the kinetic energy (part a)

The flywheel is a **macroscopic rigid body rotating** about a fixed axis. Its centre of mass does not translate, and no atomic-level oscillations are being described. This is therefore **rotational kinetic energy** — one of the three macroscopic modes identified in L0:
- Translational: centre-of-mass motion through space
- **Rotational: spinning about an axis** ← this case
- Vibrational: oscillatory motion of atoms about lattice sites (an internal/microscopic KE)

## Step 2 — Calculate rotational KE (part b)

The rotational kinetic energy of a rigid body is
$$\text{KE}_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,I\,\omega^2$$

Substituting the given values:
$$\text{KE}_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.18\text{ kg·m}^2 \times (250\text{ rad/s})^2$$
$$= 0.09 \times 62{,}500$$
$$= \boxed{5{,}625\text{ J}}$$

**Units check:** $\text{kg·m}^2 \times (\text{rad/s})^2 = \text{kg·m}^2/\text{s}^2 = \text{J}$ ✓

## Step 3 — Temperature rise from energy conversion (part c)

All rotational KE converts to internal energy $\Delta U$ of the flywheel. By the First Law, with no heat leaving and no other work:
$$\Delta U = Q + W = 0 + W_{\text{brake}} = \text{KE}_{\text{rot}} = 5{,}625\text{ J}$$

The relationship between internal energy change and temperature rise for a solid at constant pressure is
$$\Delta U \approx \Delta H = m\,c\,\Delta T$$

(For condensed phases $C_P \approx C_V$, so this approximation is excellent.)

Solving for $\Delta T$:
$$\Delta T = \frac{\Delta U}{m\,c} = \frac{5{,}625\text{ J}}{12\text{ kg} \times 500\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}}$$
$$= \frac{5{,}625}{6{,}000}$$
$$= \boxed{0.94\text{ K}}$$

## Sanity Checks
- **Order of magnitude:** a 12 kg flywheel absorbs ~5.6 kJ; steel has $c = 500\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$, so $\Delta T \approx 5600/6000 \approx 1\text{ K}$. Very small — consistent with steel's large thermal mass. ✓
- **Energy classification:** rotational KE → internal energy (random molecular motion) is exactly the conversion described in L0's framework of macroscopic vs. microscopic energy.
L0|easy.final_answer: (a) Rotational kinetic energy. (b) $\text{KE}_{\text{rot}} = 5{,}625\text{ J}$. (c) $\Delta T \approx 0.94\text{ K}$.
common_mistakes: Confusing the macroscopic rotation of the flywheel with the microscopic vibrational KE of atoms in the steel lattice. The flywheel's spin is a bulk, ordered rotational motion — the opposite of the random atomic vibrations that constitute internal energy.
Using the translational KE formula $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ with the centre-of-mass speed (which is zero for a flywheel spinning about a fixed axis) instead of the rotational form $\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$.

Forgetting to convert the full KE into $\Delta T$ via $m c \Delta T$, or using molar heat capacity (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) without first computing the number of moles — the problem provides a mass-based specific heat $c$ in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, so the formula is simply $\Delta T = \Delta U/(mc)$.

L0|medium.title: Gravitational PE to KE: Falling Steel Ball
L0|medium.statement:
A solid steel ball of mass $m = 0.85\,\text{kg}$ is dropped from rest off a tall bridge. It falls a vertical distance of $h = 45\,\text{m}$ before hitting the water surface. Neglect air resistance and treat the ball as the system.

(a) Calculate the gravitational potential energy (PE) stored in the ball relative to the water surface before it is dropped.

(b) Calculate the speed $v$ of the ball just before it hits the water.

(c) After impact, the ball comes to rest in the water and its kinetic energy is fully converted to internal energy (heat) shared between the ball and the surrounding water. If all of that thermal energy goes into the ball alone, estimate the temperature rise $\Delta T$ of the ball. The specific heat capacity of steel is $\underline{C}_P = 490\,\text{J}\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$.

Use $g = 9.81\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2}$.
L0|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Gravitational Potential Energy

Potential energy stored relative to the water surface:

$$\text{PE} = mgh = 0.85 \times 9.81 \times 45$$

$$\boxed{\text{PE} = 375.1\,\text{J}}$$

## Step 2 — Speed just before impact (part b)

With no air resistance, all PE converts to kinetic energy (KE) by the time the ball reaches the water surface:

$$\text{KE} = \text{PE} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$

Solve for $v$:

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{2\,\text{PE}}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 375.1}{0.85}}$$

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{750.2}{0.85}} = \sqrt{882.6}$$

$$\boxed{v \approx 29.7\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}}$$

**Sanity check:** Alternatively, from kinematics, $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 45} = \sqrt{882.9} \approx 29.7\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. ✓

## Step 3 — Temperature rise of the ball (part c)

After impact the ball's KE ($= 375.1\,\text{J}$) is fully dissipated as internal energy. If all of it heats the ball alone, the First Law for a closed system at constant pressure gives:

$$Q = m\,\underline{C}_P\,\Delta T$$

Here $Q = \text{KE} = 375.1\,\text{J}$. Solving for $\Delta T$:

$$\Delta T = \frac{Q}{m\,\underline{C}_P} = \frac{375.1}{0.85 \times 490}$$

$$\Delta T = \frac{375.1}{416.5}$$

$$\boxed{\Delta T \approx 0.90\,\text{K}}$$

**Interpretation:** Even though the ball falls nearly five storeys, the temperature rise is less than $1\,\text{K}$. This illustrates how large the heat capacity of metals is compared to typical mechanical energies — a direct consequence of the First Law of Thermodynamics. In reality some thermal energy would go into the water, making the actual ball temperature rise even smaller.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to convert all PE to KE in part (b) and instead trying to apply the First Law $\Delta U = Q + W$ directly without recognising that the mechanical energy balance $\text{PE} = \text{KE}$ is the correct first step for a free-fall system with no heat exchange.

In part (c), dividing by the molar heat capacity (in $\text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$) instead of the specific (mass-based) heat capacity, which would require first converting the ball mass to moles — an unnecessary complication avoided by using $\underline{C}_P$ in $\text{J}\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$ directly.

Confusing internal energy $U$ with heat $Q$: students sometimes write $\Delta U = \Delta T$ without including $m\,\underline{C}_P$, or forget that the kinetic energy of the ball's centre of mass is distinct from the microscopic internal (thermal) energy of its atoms — the conversion of bulk KE to microscopic thermal energy upon impact is exactly what the First Law tracks.

L0|medium.title: Boundary Classification and Energy Transfer in a Copper Distillation Unit
L0|medium.statement:
A copper distillation unit operates at steady state. An engineer is analysing several sub-systems within the plant and must classify them correctly before applying thermodynamic laws.

**Part (a) — System classification.** A sealed, rigid, perfectly insulated copper pressure vessel contains superheated steam at 400 K and 5 atm. Classify this vessel as isolated, closed, or open. Justify your answer using the definitions of matter and energy exchange across the boundary.

**Part (b) — Intensive vs. extensive.** The engineer measures the internal energy of the steam in the vessel to be $U_1 = 120$ kJ. A second, identical vessel (same $T$, $P$, and amount of steam) is connected and the partition removed. Without doing any calculation, state and justify the new internal energy $U_2$ and the temperature $T_2$ of the combined system.

**Part (c) — Work calculation.** Separately, 0.50 mol of an ideal gas inside a small piston-cylinder device is compressed reversibly at constant pressure $P = 3.0 \times 10^5$ Pa. The volume decreases from $V_i = 4.15 \times 10^{-3}$ m$^3$ to $V_f = 2.49 \times 10^{-3}$ m$^3$. Using the MS1016 sign convention ($\Delta U = Q + W$, where $W$ is work done **on** the system), calculate the work $W$ done on the gas during this compression.
L0|medium.solution:
## Part (a) — System classification

Apply the three-way classification from L0 §0.4:

| System type | Matter exchange? | Energy exchange? |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Isolated | ✗ | ✗ |
| Closed | ✗ | ✓ |
| Open | ✓ | ✓ |

The vessel is:
- **Rigid** → no moving parts, so no mechanical work can cross the boundary ($\delta W_{PV} = 0$).
- **Perfectly insulated** → no heat crosses the boundary ($\delta Q = 0$).
- **Sealed** → no matter enters or leaves.

All three pathways for exchange are blocked. Therefore the vessel is an **isolated system**.

## Part (b) — Intensive vs. extensive

**Internal energy $U$** is an *extensive* property — it scales with the size (amount of matter) of the system. Combining two identical systems doubles the amount of matter, so:

$$U_2 = U_1 + U_1 = 2 \times 120\,\text{kJ} = \boxed{240\,\text{kJ}}$$

**Temperature $T$** is an *intensive* property — it does not scale with system size. The two sub-systems were at the same $T$ before the partition was removed, so no heat flows between them. The temperature of the combined system is unchanged:

$$T_2 = T_1 = \boxed{400\,\text{K}}$$

This is also consistent with the Zeroth Law: two systems in thermal equilibrium with each other (both at 400 K) are in equilibrium when combined — no temperature change results.

## Part (c) — Work done on the gas

**Step 1 — Identify the process and the formula.**

The process is a *reversible*, *isobaric* (constant pressure) compression. The reversible work done **on** the system is (L0 §0.7 and L1 §1.4):

$$\delta W = -P\,\mathrm{d}V \quad\Longrightarrow\quad W = -P\,(V_f - V_i) = -P\,\Delta V$$

**Step 2 — Compute $\Delta V$.**

$$\Delta V = V_f - V_i = 2.49 \times 10^{-3} - 4.15 \times 10^{-3} = -1.66 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3$$

(Negative because the gas is being compressed — volume decreases.)

**Step 3 — Compute $W$.**

$$W = -P\,\Delta V = -(3.0 \times 10^5\,\text{Pa}) \times (-1.66 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3)$$

$$W = 3.0 \times 10^5 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{J}$$

$$\boxed{W = +498\,\text{J} \approx +0.50\,\text{kJ}}$$

**Step 4 — Sanity check.**

- $W > 0$: positive work done **on** the gas. This is correct for compression under our MS1016 convention ($\Delta U = Q + W$, $W > 0$ means work added to system). ✓
- Units: $\text{Pa} \times \text{m}^3 = \text{N/m}^2 \times \text{m}^3 = \text{N}\cdot\text{m} = \text{J}$. ✓
- The number of moles (0.50 mol) is not needed for the $P\Delta V$ work calculation — it would be needed if we wanted $\Delta U$ or $Q$. Providing it in the problem tests whether students recognise what data is relevant.
L0|medium.final_answer: (a) Isolated system. (b) $U_2 = 240$ kJ; $T_2 = 400$ K. (c) $W = +498$ J (work done on the gas).
common_mistakes: **Sign error on work:** Writing $W = P\Delta V$ (without the negative sign) and getting $W = -498$ J. Under the MS1016 convention $\delta W = -P\,\mathrm{d}V$, so compression ($\Delta V < 0$) must give $W > 0$. Students who forget the sign convention flip the answer.

**Classifying the vessel as 'closed' instead of 'isolated':** A closed system can still exchange energy (heat or work) with its surroundings. Because the vessel is both perfectly insulated *and* rigid, energy exchange is also blocked — making it isolated, not merely closed. Students often stop at 'sealed = closed' without checking the energy-exchange conditions.

**Treating temperature as extensive:** Doubling the system does not double the temperature. Students sometimes write $T_2 = 2 \times 400 = 800$ K by analogy with the internal energy calculation, confusing an intensive property ($T$) with an extensive one ($U$).

L0|medium.title: Kinetic Energy Modes of a Gas Jet
L0|medium.statement:
A supersonic nitrogen gas (N$_2$) jet used in a materials processing chamber has the following properties at a measurement cross-section:

- Bulk (macroscopic) flow velocity: $v = 450$ m/s
- Mass flow rate: $\dot{m} = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}$ kg/s
- Temperature of the gas: $T = 320$ K
- Molar mass of N$_2$: $M = 28 \times 10^{-3}$ kg/mol
- $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$

N$_2$ is a diatomic ideal gas. At this temperature, three translational and two rotational degrees of freedom are active.

**(a)** Calculate the **macroscopic (bulk translational) kinetic energy** carried by the jet per second (in watts).

**(b)** Calculate the **average internal (molecular) kinetic energy per mole** of N$_2$ at 320 K, using the equipartition theorem. State clearly which types of molecular motion contribute.

**(c)** An engineering student claims: *"The internal molecular kinetic energy of the gas is the same thing as the bulk kinetic energy of the jet — both are just kinetic energy."* Using your numerical results, explain why this statement conflates two physically distinct quantities, and identify which belongs to the system's **internal energy** $U$.
L0|medium.solution:
## Part (a) — Macroscopic (bulk) kinetic energy per second

The bulk kinetic energy carried past the cross-section per unit time is the power associated with the directed, macroscopic motion of the gas:

$$\dot{E}_\text{KE,bulk} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\dot{m}\,v^2$$

Substituting:

$$\dot{E}_\text{KE,bulk} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times (3.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg/s}) \times (450\,\text{m/s})^2$$

$$= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 3.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 202{,}500$$

$$= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 607.5 = \boxed{303.75 \approx 304\,\text{W}}$$

This is the rate at which **ordered, directed** kinetic energy flows with the jet.

---

## Part (b) — Internal (molecular) kinetic energy per mole

By the **equipartition theorem**, each active quadratic degree of freedom contributes $\tfrac{1}{2}k_BT$ per molecule, or $\tfrac{1}{2}RT$ per mole.

For diatomic N$_2$ at 320 K, five degrees of freedom are active:

| Mode | Type | Contribution (per mole) |
|---|---|---|
| $x$, $y$, $z$ translation | Translational KE | $3 \times \tfrac{1}{2}RT$ |
| 2 rotational axes | Rotational KE | $2 \times \tfrac{1}{2}RT$ |
| **Total** | | $\tfrac{5}{2}RT$ |

(Vibrational modes are frozen out at 320 K for N$_2$, consistent with $C_V = \tfrac{5}{2}R$.)

$$U_\text{mol,KE} = \frac{5}{2}RT = \frac{5}{2} \times 8.314 \times 320$$

$$= 2.5 \times 8.314 \times 320 = 2.5 \times 2660.5$$

$$= \boxed{6{,}651\,\text{J/mol} \approx 6.65\,\text{kJ/mol}}$$

This represents the **random, disordered** thermal kinetic energy of individual molecules — translating, rotating — averaged over all directions.

---

## Part (c) — Distinguishing bulk KE from internal molecular KE

**Numerically:**

Convert bulk KE to a per-mole basis for a fair comparison. The mass flow rate corresponds to a molar flow rate of:

$$\dot{n} = \frac{\dot{m}}{M} = \frac{3.0 \times 10^{-3}}{28 \times 10^{-3}} = 0.1071\,\text{mol/s}$$

Bulk KE per mole of flowing gas:

$$E_\text{KE,bulk per mol} = \frac{\dot{E}_\text{KE,bulk}}{\dot{n}} = \frac{303.75}{0.1071} \approx 2{,}836\,\text{J/mol}$$

Internal molecular KE per mole: **6,651 J/mol**

The two quantities differ by more than a factor of two and arise from completely different physics:

| Quantity | Physical origin | Macroscopic or microscopic? | Belongs to $U$? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bulk KE ($\tfrac{1}{2}\dot{m}v^2/\dot{n}$) | **Ordered, directed** centre-of-mass motion of the whole gas parcel | Macroscopic (observable flow) | **No** — it is an external kinetic energy of the system as a whole |
| Internal molecular KE ($\tfrac{5}{2}RT$) | **Random, disordered** translational + rotational motion of individual molecules | Microscopic (thermal) | **Yes** — it is part of the internal energy $U$ |

The student's claim is incorrect. The bulk jet velocity describes how fast the **centre of mass** of the gas is moving — this is a macroscopic property analogous to a moving block of metal. The molecular kinetic energy describes the **thermal agitation** of individual N$_2$ molecules relative to their own centre of mass. Only the latter contributes to the system's internal energy $U$, which is the sum of all microscopic kinetic and potential energies. As noted in L0, a gas in a moving container has both macroscopic KE (of the container + gas as a whole) *and* internal energy (thermal motion of molecules); they are distinct and must not be added without care.
L0|medium.final_answer: (a) $\dot{E}_\text{KE,bulk} \approx 304$ W; (b) $U_\text{mol,KE} = \tfrac{5}{2}RT \approx 6{,}651$ J/mol; (c) Bulk KE is ordered macroscopic motion (not part of $U$); internal molecular KE is disordered thermal motion (part of $U$).
common_mistakes: Confusing bulk (macroscopic) kinetic energy with internal (molecular) kinetic energy — the student error described in part (c). Both are 'kinetic energy' in name but they are physically and thermodynamically distinct quantities.

Using the wrong number of degrees of freedom: e.g. including vibrational modes for N₂ at 320 K (giving $\tfrac{7}{2}RT$ instead of $\tfrac{5}{2}RT$). At moderate temperatures, vibrational modes of diatomic gases are frozen out and only translation (3) and rotation (2) are active.
Forgetting to convert the mass flow rate to a molar flow rate when computing bulk KE per mole, leading to unit errors or an incorrect comparison with the molar internal energy.

L0|medium.title: Soap Film Work and First Law at Constant Temperature
L0|medium.statement:
A rectangular wire frame is used to form a soap film. The frame has a movable crossbar of length $L = 0.04\,\text{m}$. The surface tension of the soap solution is $\sigma = 0.035\,\text{N\,m}^{-1}$.

The crossbar is pushed **inward** (reducing the film area) by a distance $\mathrm{d}x = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}$ in a slow, quasi-static process at constant temperature.

**(a)** Write an expression for the reversible work done **by the soap film** on the crossbar during this compression, and calculate its numerical value. Recall that a soap film has **two** surfaces.

**(b)** The process is isothermal and the internal energy of the soap film does not change during this quasi-static compression at constant temperature (analogous to an ideal system). Using the First Law $\Delta U = Q + W$, where $W$ is work done **on** the system, determine the heat $Q$ exchanged by the soap film with its surroundings. State whether heat flows **into** or **out of** the soap film.

**(c)** Classify the soap film (just the film itself, not the frame) as an **open**, **closed**, or **isolated** system, and state whether surface tension work is a **path** function or a **state** function.
L0|medium.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Work done **by** the soap film

A soap film has **two** liquid–air interfaces, so the effective force exerted by the film on the crossbar is

$$F = 2\sigma L$$

When the crossbar is pushed **inward** by $\mathrm{d}x$, the film area **decreases** ($\mathrm{d}x > 0$ inward means the film contracts). The film resists this compression, so the film does **negative** work on the crossbar (the external agent does positive work on the film).

The work done **by** the soap film on the crossbar:

$$\delta W_\text{by film} = -2\sigma L\,\mathrm{d}x$$

(Negative because the film force opposes the inward displacement.)

Substituting values:

$$\delta W_\text{by film} = -2 \times 0.035\,\text{N\,m}^{-1} \times 0.04\,\text{m} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}$$

$$= -2 \times 0.035 \times 0.04 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{J}$$

$$\boxed{\delta W_\text{by film} = -5.6 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{J}}$$

The negative sign confirms the film loses energy to compression — the agent **does work on** the film.

### Part (b) — Heat exchanged via the First Law

Under our course convention, the First Law is

$$\Delta U = Q + W$$

where $W$ is work done **on** the system and $Q > 0$ means heat **absorbed by** the system.

Work done **on** the soap film (opposite sign to the work done by the film):

$$W = +2\sigma L\,\mathrm{d}x = +5.6 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{J}$$

Given that $\Delta U = 0$ (isothermal, ideal-like film):

$$0 = Q + W$$

$$Q = -W = -5.6 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{J}$$

$$\boxed{Q = -5.6 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{J}}$$

Since $Q < 0$, heat flows **out of** the soap film into the surroundings.

**Physical interpretation:** Compressing the film does work on it. To maintain constant internal energy (constant $T$), the film must expel exactly that amount of energy as heat to the surroundings. This is directly analogous to the isothermal compression of an ideal gas.

### Part (c) — System classification and path/state function

**System type:** The soap film (just the liquid film, not the frame) is a **closed system**. No matter (soap molecules) crosses the boundary during this quasi-static process — the film merely changes shape. Energy crosses the boundary as both work (mechanical, via the crossbar) and heat (thermal, to the surroundings), which is the hallmark of a closed system.

**Path or state function:** Surface tension work $\delta W_\text{surf} = 2\sigma\,L\,\mathrm{d}x$ is a **path function**. The total work depends on *how* the area changes (the sequence of intermediate states), not just the initial and final areas. This is exactly analogous to $PV$ expansion work — both are inexact differentials, written with $\delta$ rather than $\mathrm{d}$.
L0|medium.final_answer: (a) $\delta W_\text{by film} = -5.6 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{J}$; (b) $Q = -5.6 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{J}$ (heat flows **out**); (c) closed system; surface tension work is a **path function**.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the factor of 2 for the two surfaces of the soap film, giving an answer half the correct magnitude for both the work and the heat.

Using the wrong sign convention: writing $W$ as work done **by** the system and then applying $\Delta U = Q + W$ without adjusting the sign, leading to $Q = +5.6 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{J}$ (wrong direction of heat flow). The course convention is $\Delta U = Q + W$ with $W$ = work done **on** the system.

Classifying surface tension work as a state function because $\sigma$ and $L$ appear to be fixed properties, rather than recognising that work always depends on the path (how $x$ changes) and is an inexact differential.

L0|medium.title: Elastically Stretched Rubber Band
L0|medium.statement:
A rubber band is stretched adiabatically and reversibly by a tensile force $F$ over a small extension $\mathrm{d}L$. The rubber band is then clamped (held at constant length) while it absorbs a small quantity of heat $\delta Q = 12\text{ J}$ from the surroundings.

(a) Write the differential form of the First Law for the stretching step, identifying the work term explicitly. Use the sign convention $\Delta U = Q + W$ (work done **on** the system is positive).

(b) Given that during the adiabatic stretching step the tensile force is $F = 8\text{ N}$ and the extension is $\mathrm{d}L = 0.015\text{ m}$, calculate the change in internal energy $\mathrm{d}U$ of the rubber band during stretching.

(c) After clamping (constant length, so $\mathrm{d}L = 0$), the rubber band absorbs $\delta Q = 12\text{ J}$. What is the change in internal energy during this second step? What work is done on the rubber band in this step?
L0|medium.solution:
## Part (a) — First Law for a stretched elastic solid

For a system that can exchange both heat and elastic work, the appropriate form of the First Law is:

$$\mathrm{d}U = \delta Q + \delta W$$

The work done **on** the rubber band when it is stretched by an external force $F$ through an extension $\mathrm{d}L$ is:

$$\delta W = +F\,\mathrm{d}L$$

(positive because the external agent does work **on** the system by pulling it — analogous to compression work $-P\,\mathrm{d}V$ but for a tensile system).

So the First Law for the rubber band is:

$$\boxed{\mathrm{d}U = \delta Q + F\,\mathrm{d}L}$$

**Note on sign:** For a gas, compression ($\mathrm{d}V < 0$) gives $\delta W = -P\,\mathrm{d}V > 0$ (work done on the gas). For a rod or rubber band, extension ($\mathrm{d}L > 0$) under a tensile force gives $\delta W = F\,\mathrm{d}L > 0$ (work done on the solid). Both follow the same logic: the external agent does positive work on the system.

---

## Part (b) — Adiabatic stretching step

The process is **adiabatic**, so $\delta Q = 0$. Substituting into the First Law:

$$\mathrm{d}U = 0 + F\,\mathrm{d}L = F\,\mathrm{d}L$$

Substituting the given values:

$$\mathrm{d}U = (8\text{ N})(0.015\text{ m})$$

$$\boxed{\mathrm{d}U = 0.12\text{ J}}$$

**Interpretation:** All of the elastic work done by the external agent goes directly into increasing the internal energy of the rubber band (since no heat can leave an adiabatic system). The rubber band warms slightly — consistent with the observed experimental fact that stretching rubber adiabatically raises its temperature.

---

## Part (c) — Constant-length (isometric) heating step

Once clamped, $\mathrm{d}L = 0$, so the elastic work term vanishes:

$$\delta W = F\,\mathrm{d}L = F \times 0 = 0$$

The First Law then reduces to:

$$\mathrm{d}U = \delta Q + 0 = \delta Q$$

With $\delta Q = +12\text{ J}$ (heat **absorbed** by the system, so positive by our convention):

$$\boxed{\mathrm{d}U = 12\text{ J}}$$

The work done on the rubber band in this step is:

$$\boxed{W = 0\text{ J}}$$

**Interpretation:** At constant length, there is no displacement and therefore no mechanical (elastic) work. All the absorbed heat goes entirely into raising the internal energy — exactly analogous to an isochoric (constant-volume) process for a gas, where $\mathrm{d}U = \delta Q_V$.
common_mistakes: Students often write $\delta W = -F\,\mathrm{d}L$ for stretching by analogy with the gas-compression sign, forgetting that the analogue of compression (work **on** the system) for an elastic body is extension under tension — both give $\delta W > 0$ under the work-on convention.
In part (b), students may forget the adiabatic condition ($\delta Q = 0$) and attempt to find $\mathrm{d}U$ using only heat, obtaining zero — confusing 'no heat' with 'no energy change'.

In part (c), students sometimes include the clamping force as doing work, arguing $W = F \times 0 \neq 0$. Work requires actual displacement; if $\mathrm{d}L = 0$, no work is done regardless of how large $F$ is.

L0|medium.title: Isothermal Compression of Nitrogen Gas
L0|medium.statement:
A sealed, rigid-walled cylinder initially contains $n = 2.5$ mol of nitrogen gas (N$_2$, treat as ideal and diatomic) at temperature $T_1 = 350$ K and pressure $P_1 = 1.5$ atm. The cylinder is then fitted with a frictionless, massless piston that slowly compresses the gas **isothermally** (at constant $T = 350$ K) until the final pressure is $P_2 = 6.0$ atm.

**(a)** Classify the cylinder (with its piston) as an **open**, **closed**, or **isolated** system, and justify your classification in terms of matter and energy exchange.

**(b)** The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. State whether $\Delta U$ for this process is positive, negative, or zero, and explain why.

**(c)** Using the First Law $\Delta U = Q + W$ (where $W$ is work done **on** the system), and the result from part (b), determine the heat $Q$ transferred during the compression. State whether heat flows **into** or **out of** the system.

**(d)** Calculate the work $W$ done **on** the gas during this isothermal reversible compression. Use $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.
L0|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Classify the system (Part a)

The cylinder + piston contains a fixed amount of gas: **no matter crosses the boundary**. However, the piston can move (work crosses the boundary) and the cylinder walls can conduct heat (thermal interaction with surroundings). Therefore it is a **closed system** — energy (both heat and work) can cross the boundary, but matter cannot.

---

## Step 2 — Change in internal energy (Part b)

For an **ideal gas**, internal energy $U$ depends **only on temperature** (a key property stated in L0/L1):
$$\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = 0$$

Since the process is **isothermal** ($T = $ constant $= 350$ K), there is no change in temperature and therefore:
$$\boxed{\Delta U = 0}$$

Physically, the kinetic energies of the N$_2$ molecules are unchanged because temperature (which measures average molecular kinetic energy) has not changed.

---

## Step 3 — Heat transferred (Part c)

Apply the First Law with $\Delta U = Q + W$:
$$0 = Q + W \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q = -W$$

Because work is done **on** the gas ($W > 0$, as shown in Step 4), we get $Q < 0$: **heat flows out of the system** into the surroundings. This is physically required to keep the gas at the same temperature while it is being compressed — the surroundings must absorb the energy added by the compression work.

---

## Step 4 — Work done on the gas (Part d)

For a **reversible isothermal** compression of an ideal gas, the work done **on** the system is:
$$W = -\int_{V_1}^{V_2} P\,\mathrm{d}V$$

For an ideal gas, $P = nRT/V$, so:
$$W = -\int_{V_1}^{V_2} \frac{nRT}{V}\,\mathrm{d}V = -nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$$

Using the ideal gas law at constant $T$: $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$, so $V_2/V_1 = P_1/P_2$. Substitute:
$$W = -nRT\ln\frac{P_1}{P_2} = nRT\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}$$

Now substitute numbers:
$$W = (2.5\,\text{mol})(8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1})(350\,\text{K})\ln\!\left(\frac{6.0}{1.5}\right)$$

$$W = (2.5)(8.314)(350)\ln(4)$$

$$W = 7274.75 \times 1.3863$$

$$\boxed{W \approx +10{,}085\,\text{J} \approx +10.1\,\text{kJ}}$$

The positive sign confirms work is done **on** the gas (compression).

**Therefore, from Part c:**
$$Q = -W \approx -10.1\,\text{kJ}$$

The system releases approximately **10.1 kJ of heat** to the surroundings during the isothermal compression.

---

## Sanity Check

- Compression always requires positive work input — $W > 0$ ✓
- Isothermal compression of an ideal gas must release heat to the surroundings to maintain constant $T$ — $Q < 0$ ✓
- $|Q| = |W|$ because $\Delta U = 0$ for isothermal ideal gas ✓
- The diatomic nature of N$_2$ is irrelevant here because $C_V$ and $C_P$ only matter when $T$ changes; since $\Delta T = 0$, neither heat capacity is needed ✓
L0|medium.final_answer: $W \approx +10.1\,\text{kJ}$ (work done on gas); $Q \approx -10.1\,\text{kJ}$ (heat released to surroundings); $\Delta U = 0$
common_mistakes: **Forgetting that $\Delta U = 0$ for an isothermal ideal gas process.** Students often calculate $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$ and then incorrectly use a non-zero $\Delta T$, or assume that compression must always increase internal energy regardless of temperature constraint.

**Sign error in the work formula.** Using $W = nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$ directly without converting the volume ratio to a pressure ratio, and incorrectly writing $\ln(P_2/P_1)$ as negative — forgetting that $V_2 < V_1$ so $\ln(V_2/V_1) < 0$, which gives $W > 0$ (work on system). The safest path is to substitute $V_2/V_1 = P_1/P_2$ explicitly.

**Invoking $C_V$ or $C_P$ for N$_2$.** Because N$_2$ is diatomic, students may try to use $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$ to compute $\Delta U$. This is unnecessary and misleading: for an isothermal process $\Delta T = 0$, so $n C_V \Delta T = 0$ regardless of which heat capacity is used. The diatomic nature of the gas is a red herring in this problem.

L0|medium.title: Molar Volume and Specific Properties of Titanium
L0|medium.statement:
Titanium (Ti) is widely used in aerospace applications due to its high strength-to-weight ratio. Given the following data for elemental titanium:

- Molar mass: $M = 47.87$ g/mol
- Density: $\rho = 4.51$ g/cm$^3$
- A sample of titanium has a total mass of $m = 250$ g

**(a)** Calculate the molar volume $\underline{V}$ of titanium in m$^3$/mol.

**(b)** Calculate the total volume $V_\text{total}$ of the sample in m$^3$.

**(c)** Calculate the number of moles $n$ in the sample.

**(d)** A student claims that the molar volume $\underline{V}$ is an *extensive* property because it has units of m$^3$ (a volume). Is the student correct? Justify your answer by checking what happens to $\underline{V}$ when you combine two identical 250 g titanium blocks into one 500 g block.
L0|medium.solution:
## Step-by-step solution

### Part (a) — Molar volume $\underline{V}$

The molar volume is defined as molar mass divided by density:

$$\underline{V} = \frac{M}{\rho}$$

Substituting values (note: convert cm$^3$ to m$^3$ using $1\text{ cm}^3 = 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3$):

$$\underline{V} = \frac{47.87\text{ g/mol}}{4.51\text{ g/cm}^3} \times 10^{-6}\frac{\text{m}^3}{\text{cm}^3}$$

$$\underline{V} = 10.614\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol} \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3/\text{cm}^3$$

$$\boxed{\underline{V} = 1.061 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^3/\text{mol}}$$

---

### Part (b) — Total volume $V_\text{total}$

Using the definition of density $\rho = m/V$, rearranged:

$$V_\text{total} = \frac{m}{\rho} = \frac{250\text{ g}}{4.51\text{ g/cm}^3}$$

$$V_\text{total} = 55.43\text{ cm}^3 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3/\text{cm}^3$$

$$\boxed{V_\text{total} = 5.543 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^3}$$

---

### Part (c) — Number of moles $n$

$$n = \frac{m}{M} = \frac{250\text{ g}}{47.87\text{ g/mol}}$$

$$\boxed{n = 5.222\text{ mol}}$$

**Consistency check:** $V_\text{total} = n \times \underline{V} = 5.222\text{ mol} \times 1.061 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^3/\text{mol} = 5.540 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^3$ $\approx 5.543 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^3$ ✓ (small rounding difference)

---

### Part (d) — Intensive vs. extensive classification of $\underline{V}$

The student is **incorrect**. $\underline{V}$ (molar volume) is an **intensive** property.

Recall the definitions from L0:
- An **extensive** property scales with the size (amount) of the system.
- An **intensive** property does NOT depend on the amount of material.

Applying the test: combine two identical 250 g blocks into one 500 g block.

| Quantity | Single 250 g block | Combined 500 g block | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total volume $V_\text{total}$ | $5.543 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^3$ | $1.109 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^3$ | $2\times$ → **extensive** |
| Number of moles $n$ | $5.222\text{ mol}$ | $10.444\text{ mol}$ | $2\times$ → **extensive** |
| Molar volume $\underline{V}$ | $1.061 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^3/\text{mol}$ | $1.061 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^3/\text{mol}$ | $1\times$ → **intensive** |

The molar volume is the **ratio** of two extensive quantities ($V_\text{total}/n$). As stated in L0: *the ratio of two extensive properties is intensive.* Doubling the system doubles both $V_\text{total}$ and $n$, so their ratio remains unchanged.

The confusion arises because $\underline{V}$ has units of m$^3$ — but the units alone do not determine intensive vs. extensive character. What matters is whether the value changes when you scale the system size.
L0|medium.final_answer: (a) $\underline{V} = 1.061 \times 10^{-5}$ m$^3$/mol; (b) $V_\text{total} = 5.543 \times 10^{-5}$ m$^3$; (c) $n = 5.22$ mol; (d) The student is incorrect — molar volume is intensive (ratio of two extensives; unchanged when system is doubled).
common_mistakes: Confusing units with extensivity: students see 'm³' in the units of molar volume and conclude it must be extensive, forgetting that intensive vs. extensive depends on system-size scaling, not on the type of unit.
Forgetting to convert cm³ to m³ when computing molar volume, leaving the answer in cm³/mol and then using it inconsistently with SI units in subsequent calculations.

Applying the intensive/extensive test incorrectly by checking only total volume (which does double) without also checking moles (which also double), and therefore concluding the ratio changes when it does not.

L0|medium.title: Boundary Work and First Law for Soap Film Expansion
L0|medium.statement:
A rectangular soap film is held in a wire frame with dimensions $L = 0.08\text{ m}$ (fixed side) and an initial width $x_1 = 0.04\text{ m}$. A movable wire on one end is slowly pulled outward in a quasi-static (reversible) process until the width increases to $x_2 = 0.09\text{ m}$. The surface tension of the soap solution is $\sigma = 0.035\text{ N/m}$.

**(a)** Calculate the work done **on** the soap film during this process, using the sign convention $\Delta U = Q + W$.

**(b)** The process is carried out under conditions where the internal energy of the soap film remains unchanged ($\Delta U = 0$). Determine the heat flow $Q$ for the process, and state whether heat is absorbed by the film or released to the surroundings.
L0|medium.solution:
## Setup and Conventions

We use the MS1016 sign convention throughout:
$$\Delta U = Q + W$$
where $W > 0$ means work is done **on** the system, and $Q > 0$ means heat is **absorbed** by the system.

A soap film has **two surfaces** (front and back), so the total surface area for a film of width $x$ and fixed length $L$ is:
$$A = 2Lx$$

---

## Part (a) — Work Done on the Film

**Step 1 — Express the work done by the system.**

For a soap film, the work done **by** the film when its area increases by $\mathrm{d}A$ against surface tension $\sigma$ is:
$$\delta W_\text{by system} = \sigma\,\mathrm{d}A$$

Since the area changes as $\mathrm{d}A = 2L\,\mathrm{d}x$ (two surfaces, fixed $L$):
$$\delta W_\text{by system} = 2\sigma L\,\mathrm{d}x$$

**Step 2 — Integrate over the displacement.**

The total work done **by** the system as $x$ goes from $x_1$ to $x_2$:
$$W_\text{by system} = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} 2\sigma L\,\mathrm{d}x = 2\sigma L(x_2 - x_1)$$

Substituting values:
$$W_\text{by system} = 2 \times 0.035 \times 0.08 \times (0.09 - 0.04)$$
$$= 2 \times 0.035 \times 0.08 \times 0.05$$
$$= 2 \times 1.4 \times 10^{-4}$$
$$= 2.8 \times 10^{-4}\text{ J}$$

**Step 3 — Apply the sign convention.**

Under $\Delta U = Q + W$, the work done **on** the system is the negative of the work done **by** the system (because expanding the film requires the external agent to do work on it — the film pulls back against the external force):
$$W = -W_\text{by system} = -(2.8 \times 10^{-4}) = \boxed{-2.8 \times 10^{-4}\text{ J}}$$

Wait — let us be careful about direction. The movable wire is pulled **outward** by an external agent. The soap film (system) resists this expansion with a surface-tension force directed **inward** (opposing the motion). The external agent does positive work on the wire, but the soap film itself **does positive work** on the surroundings by virtue of... actually, no: the film must be *stretched* by the external agent against its surface tension. The external force and displacement are in the **same** direction, so the external agent does **positive** work on the film.

More carefully: the restoring force of the film on the wire is $F_\text{film} = -2\sigma L$ (directed inward, opposing extension). The force the external agent applies is $F_\text{ext} = +2\sigma L$ (quasi-static). Work done **by the external agent on the system** is:
$$W = F_\text{ext} \cdot (x_2 - x_1) = 2\sigma L (x_2 - x_1) = +2.8\times10^{-4}\text{ J}$$

So under our convention, **work done on the film** is:
$$\boxed{W = +2.8 \times 10^{-4}\text{ J}}$$

This is positive, consistent with energy being added to the film by the external agent stretching it.

---

## Part (b) — Heat Flow

Apply the First Law with $\Delta U = 0$:
$$\Delta U = Q + W = 0$$
$$Q = -W = -2.8 \times 10^{-4}\text{ J}$$

$$\boxed{Q = -2.8 \times 10^{-4}\text{ J}}$$

**Interpretation:** $Q < 0$ means the soap film **releases heat to the surroundings**. As the film is stretched and its surface area increases, the external agent does $+2.8\times10^{-4}$ J of work on it; since $\Delta U = 0$ (internal energy unchanged), the film must simultaneously release exactly that much energy as heat. This is analogous to an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas: all work input exits as heat.
L0|medium.final_answer: (a) $W = +2.8 \times 10^{-4}\text{ J}$ (work done on the film); (b) $Q = -2.8 \times 10^{-4}\text{ J}$ (heat released by the film to the surroundings).
common_mistakes: **Forgetting the two surfaces of the soap film.** A soap film has a front and back surface, so the total area is $A = 2Lx$, not $Lx$. Using only one surface halves the answer.

**Sign confusion between work done by vs. work done on the system.** Under the MS1016 convention $\Delta U = Q + W$, $W$ is work done **on** the system. Stretching the film requires the external agent to do positive work on it, so $W > 0$. Students who apply $W = -\int P\,\mathrm{d}V$ thinking the film is doing positive work on the surroundings will arrive at $W < 0$ incorrectly.

**Assuming $Q = 0$ because $\Delta U = 0$.** Some students confuse $\Delta U = 0$ with an adiabatic process. If $\Delta U = 0$ but $W \neq 0$, then by the First Law $Q = -W \neq 0$. An adiabatic process has $Q = 0$ (not $\Delta U = 0$).  These are distinct conditions.

L0|medium.title: Kinetic Energy Mode Identification and Internal Energy
L0|medium.statement:
A sealed rigid container holds a sample of nitrogen gas (N$_2$) at 350 K. A separate sealed rigid container holds a sample of argon gas (Ar) at the same temperature.

(a) Identify the dominant kinetic energy modes available to each gas at 350 K, explaining why they differ.

(b) Both samples contain exactly 2 mol of gas. Using the equipartition principle, calculate the internal energy $U$ stored in each sample at 350 K. Express your answers in joules.

(c) The argon container is connected to a perfectly rigid, perfectly insulating chamber of equal volume that is initially evacuated. The valve is opened and the argon expands to fill both chambers. State whether $\Delta U$, $Q$, and $W$ are each positive, negative, or zero for this expansion process, and justify each answer using the First Law $\Delta U = Q + W$.

Given: $R = 8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$; $T = 350$ K; $n = 2$ mol for each gas.
L0|medium.solution:
## Part (a) — Kinetic Energy Modes

**Argon (Ar)** is a monatomic noble gas. Its atoms have no internal structure capable of rotation or vibration. The only accessible kinetic energy mode at 350 K is:
- **Translational** (3 degrees of freedom: motion in $x$, $y$, $z$).

Total degrees of freedom for Ar: $f = 3$.

**Nitrogen (N$_2$)** is a diatomic molecule. At 350 K (well above the quantum threshold for rotation but well below vibrational excitation temperatures ~3400 K for N$_2$), the accessible modes are:
- **Translational** (3 degrees of freedom).
- **Rotational** (2 degrees of freedom — rotation about the two axes perpendicular to the bond axis; rotation about the bond axis itself has negligible moment of inertia and is not thermally excited classically).

Vibrational modes are **not** significantly populated at 350 K for N$_2$ (the vibrational temperature $\Theta_\text{vib} \approx 3400$ K $\gg 350$ K).

Total degrees of freedom for N$_2$: $f = 5$.

## Part (b) — Internal Energy via Equipartition

By the equipartition theorem, each quadratic degree of freedom contributes $\frac{1}{2}RT$ per mole to the internal energy.

$$U = n \cdot \frac{f}{2} RT$$

**Argon** ($f = 3$, monatomic, $C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$):

$$U_\text{Ar} = 2 \times \frac{3}{2} \times 8.314 \times 350$$

$$= 2 \times 1.5 \times 2909.9$$

$$= 2 \times 4364.9 = \boxed{8730 \text{ J}}$$

**Nitrogen** ($f = 5$, diatomic, $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$):

$$U_\text{N_2} = 2 \times \frac{5}{2} \times 8.314 \times 350$$

$$= 2 \times 2.5 \times 2909.9$$

$$= 2 \times 7274.7 = \boxed{14{,}549 \text{ J}}$$

So nitrogen stores approximately **67% more internal energy** than argon at the same $T$ and $n$, purely because of the additional rotational modes.

## Part (c) — Free Expansion of Argon: First Law Analysis

The argon expands into a vacuum (evacuated rigid chamber). Analysing each term:

**Work $W$ done on the system:**

The expanding gas pushes against the vacuum. There is no opposing pressure (the chamber is evacuated), so no force acts through any displacement:
$$\delta W = -P_\text{ext}\,dV = -(0)\,dV = 0$$
$$\boxed{W = 0}$$

**Heat $Q$:**

The container walls are perfectly insulating (adiabatic boundary). No heat crosses the boundary:
$$\boxed{Q = 0}$$

**Internal energy change $\Delta U$:**

Apply the First Law:
$$\Delta U = Q + W = 0 + 0 = 0$$
$$\boxed{\Delta U = 0}$$

**Consistency check:** For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature: $U = U(T)$. Since $\Delta U = 0$, the temperature of the argon does not change after the free expansion — a result known as the Joule expansion. This is consistent with the ideal-gas property $\left(\partial U/\partial V\right)_T = 0$ (from L1).
L0|medium.final_answer: (a) Ar: translational only (3 DOF); N$_2$: translational + rotational (5 DOF) at 350 K. (b) $U_\text{Ar} = 8730$ J; $U_{\text{N}_2} = 14{,}549$ J. (c) $W = 0$ (expansion into vacuum), $Q = 0$ (adiabatic walls), $\Delta U = 0$ (by First Law).
common_mistakes: Assigning vibrational degrees of freedom to N$_2$ at 350 K — vibrational modes are only excited at temperatures approaching the vibrational temperature (~3400 K for N$_2$), so they should not be included at 350 K.

Assuming work is done during the free expansion because the gas volume increases — students forget that $W = -P_\text{ext}\,dV$ and the external pressure is zero (vacuum), so no work is done regardless of $\Delta V$.
Concluding that $\Delta U > 0$ because 'the gas fills more space' — internal energy of an ideal gas is a function of temperature only, not volume; since $Q = W = 0$, $\Delta U$ must be zero.

L0|medium.title: Classifying Intensive vs. Extensive Properties of a Liquid Alloy
L0|medium.statement:
A sealed steel crucible contains $n = 2.5$ mol of a liquid binary alloy (components A and B) at temperature $T = 1200$ K and pressure $P = 1$ atm. The alloy has a total internal energy $U = 18{,}500$ J, a total volume $V = 38.0$ cm$^3$, and a total entropy $S = 28.4$ J/K.

An identical second crucible — same material, same composition, same $T$ and $P$, containing another 2.5 mol of the same alloy — is combined with the first by opening a valve between them (no work done, no heat lost, pressure stays at 1 atm throughout).

(a) State whether each of the following properties is **intensive** or **extensive**, and give a one-sentence physical justification for each:
- Temperature $T$
- Total internal energy $U$
- Molar entropy $\underline{S} = S/n$
- Pressure $P$
- Total volume $V$

(b) For each property listed in (a), calculate its value in the **combined** system after the valve is opened. Where the quantity is intensive, explain why no calculation is needed.

(c) Compute the molar volume $\underline{V}$ (in cm$^3$/mol) of the combined system and confirm it is the same as for either crucible alone.
L0|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Classify each property as intensive or extensive

The defining test: if you double the amount of matter (at the same $T$, $P$, composition), does the property double? If yes → **extensive**. If no → **intensive**.

| Property | Classification | Physical reason |
|---|---|---|
| $T$ | **Intensive** | Temperature is the average molecular kinetic energy per degree of freedom — it does not accumulate when you add more identical matter. |
| $U$ | **Extensive** | Internal energy is the *total* of all molecular kinetic and potential energies; adding more molecules adds more energy. |
| $\underline{S} = S/n$ | **Intensive** | Dividing an extensive quantity (entropy $S$) by another extensive quantity (moles $n$) gives an intensive ratio — independent of system size. |
| $P$ | **Intensive** | Pressure is force per unit area — a bulk, size-independent property; identical blocks of the same fluid have the same pressure. |
| $V$ | **Extensive** | Volume scales directly with the amount of matter at fixed $T$ and $P$. |

---

## Step 2 — Values in the combined system

Each crucible contains: $n_1 = 2.5$ mol, $U_1 = 18{,}500$ J, $V_1 = 38.0$ cm$^3$, $S_1 = 28.4$ J/K, at $T_1 = 1200$ K, $P_1 = 1$ atm.

The second crucible is **identical** in every way, so $n_2 = 2.5$ mol, $U_2 = 18{,}500$ J, $V_2 = 38.0$ cm$^3$, $S_2 = 28.4$ J/K, $T_2 = 1200$ K, $P_2 = 1$ atm.

### Intensive properties — no calculation needed

Because $T$ and $P$ are intensive, the combined system has:
$$T_\text{combined} = 1200\text{ K}$$
$$P_\text{combined} = 1\text{ atm}$$
Joining two identical systems at the same $T$ and $P$ leaves those properties unchanged — they characterise the *state* of the matter, not the *quantity* present.

### Extensive properties — add both contributions

$$n_\text{combined} = n_1 + n_2 = 2.5 + 2.5 = 5.0\text{ mol}$$

$$U_\text{combined} = U_1 + U_2 = 18{,}500 + 18{,}500 = 37{,}000\text{ J}$$

$$V_\text{combined} = V_1 + V_2 = 38.0 + 38.0 = 76.0\text{ cm}^3$$

$$S_\text{combined} = S_1 + S_2 = 28.4 + 28.4 = 56.8\text{ J/K}$$

### Molar entropy — remains intensive

$$\underline{S}_\text{combined} = \frac{S_\text{combined}}{n_\text{combined}} = \frac{56.8\text{ J/K}}{5.0\text{ mol}} = 11.36\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

Check against single crucible:
$$\underline{S}_\text{single} = \frac{28.4}{2.5} = 11.36\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} \checkmark$$

---

## Step 3 — Compute and verify molar volume

**Single crucible:**
$$\underline{V}_\text{single} = \frac{V_1}{n_1} = \frac{38.0\text{ cm}^3}{2.5\text{ mol}} = 15.2\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol}$$

**Combined system:**
$$\underline{V}_\text{combined} = \frac{V_\text{combined}}{n_\text{combined}} = \frac{76.0\text{ cm}^3}{5.0\text{ mol}} = 15.2\text{ cm}^3/\text{mol} \checkmark$$

The molar volume is intensive: it is unchanged when two identical systems are combined. This confirms the classification — the ratio of two extensive properties ($V$ and $n$) is intensive.

---

## Summary table

| Property | Single crucible | Combined system | Changed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| $T$ (K) | 1200 | 1200 | No (intensive) |
| $P$ (atm) | 1 | 1 | No (intensive) |
| $\underline{S}$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) | 11.36 | 11.36 | No (intensive) |
| $\underline{V}$ (cm$^3$/mol) | 15.2 | 15.2 | No (intensive) |
| $U$ (J) | 18,500 | 37,000 | Yes — doubled (extensive) |
| $V$ (cm$^3$) | 38.0 | 76.0 | Yes — doubled (extensive) |
| $S$ (J/K) | 28.4 | 56.8 | Yes — doubled (extensive) |
| $n$ (mol) | 2.5 | 5.0 | Yes — doubled (extensive) |
L0|medium.final_answer: (a) $T$: intensive; $U$: extensive; $\underline{S}=S/n$: intensive; $P$: intensive; $V$: extensive. (b) Combined values: $T=1200$ K, $P=1$ atm, $\underline{S}=11.36$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ (unchanged); $U=37{,}000$ J, $V=76.0$ cm$^3$, $S=56.8$ J/K (all doubled). (c) $\underline{V}_\text{combined} = 76.0/5.0 = 15.2$ cm$^3$/mol $= \underline{V}_\text{single}$ ✓
common_mistakes: Treating entropy $S$ as intensive (because it is "disordered") — entropy is extensive; only the molar entropy $S/n$ is intensive. Students often confuse the concept of entropy as a measure of disorder with the bookkeeping fact that total entropy scales with system size.
Recalculating $T$ and $P$ by adding them — intensive properties do not add when systems are combined. Two identical baths at 1200 K joined together are still at 1200 K, not 2400 K.
