Applying $\Delta G^\circ = 0$ at exactly the boiling point and concluding the calculation is wrong — in fact, the approximation that $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are temperature-independent introduces a small error, so $\Delta G^\circ_{630} \approx 0$ (not exactly zero) is the correct expectation.

In the Gibbs–Helmholtz integration, computing $\left(-1/T\right)_{298}^{630}$ with the wrong sign, giving $+108.49$ instead of $-108.49\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, and failing to recognise the sign mismatch as an error rather than a physical result.

L3|medium.title: Gibbs Free Energy and Spontaneity for Magnetite Formation
L3|medium.statement:
The formation of magnetite (Fe$_3$O$_4$) from iron and oxygen is a key reaction in corrosion science:

$$4\,\text{Fe(s)} + 3\,\text{O}_2\text{(g)} \longrightarrow 2\,\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4\text{(s)}$$

Use the thermodynamic data below (all at 298 K, 1 atm) to answer the following:

| Species | $\Delta H_f^\circ$ (kJ/mol) | $S^\circ_{298}$ (J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Fe(s) | 0 | 27.32 |
| O$_2$(g) | 0 | 205.14 |
| Fe$_3$O$_4$(s) | $-1118.4$ | 146.40 |

**(a)** Calculate $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ and $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ for the reaction as written.

**(b)** Calculate $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K and state whether the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.

**(c)** Estimate the temperature above which the reaction becomes **non-spontaneous** (i.e. find $T^*$ where $\Delta G^\circ = 0$), assuming $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are approximately independent of temperature.
L3|medium.solution:
## Step 1 — Calculate $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$

Using Hess's Law (products minus reactants, weighted by stoichiometric coefficients):

$$\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = 2\,\Delta H_f^\circ[\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4] - 4\,\Delta H_f^\circ[\text{Fe}] - 3\,\Delta H_f^\circ[\text{O}_2]$$

$$= 2(-1118.4) - 4(0) - 3(0)$$

$$\boxed{\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = -2236.8 \text{ kJ/mol}}$$

The large negative value confirms the reaction is strongly **exothermic** — iron oxidising to magnetite releases substantial heat, consistent with observed corrosion processes.

## Step 2 — Calculate $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$

Using standard molar entropies (products minus reactants):

$$\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = 2\,S^\circ[\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4] - 4\,S^\circ[\text{Fe}] - 3\,S^\circ[\text{O}_2]$$

$$= 2(146.40) - 4(27.32) - 3(205.14)$$

$$= 292.80 - 109.28 - 615.42$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = -431.90 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

**Physical reasoning:** Three moles of O$_2$ gas (high molar entropy, ~205 J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ each) are consumed to make two moles of a solid oxide. Consuming gases to make solids always decreases entropy strongly. The negative $\Delta S^\circ$ means this reaction is entropically **unfavourable**.

## Step 3 — Calculate $\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$ at 298 K

Using the fundamental relation:

$$\Delta G^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} - T\,\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$$

Note: convert $\Delta S^\circ$ to kJ: $-431.90 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} = -0.43190 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

$$\Delta G^\circ_{298} = -2236.8 - (298)(-0.43190)$$

$$= -2236.8 + 128.71$$

$$\boxed{\Delta G^\circ_{298} = -2108.1 \text{ kJ/mol}}$$

Since $\Delta G^\circ_{298} \ll 0$, the reaction is **strongly spontaneous** at standard conditions (298 K, 1 atm O$_2$). The enthalpy term ($-2236.8$ kJ/mol) completely dominates the unfavourable entropy penalty ($+128.7$ kJ/mol at 298 K).

## Step 4 — Find the crossover temperature $T^*$

At $T^*$, $\Delta G^\circ = 0$, so:

$$0 = \Delta H^\circ - T^*\,\Delta S^\circ$$

$$T^* = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ} = \frac{-2{,}236{,}800 \text{ J/mol}}{-431.90 \text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}$$

$$\boxed{T^* \approx 5179 \text{ K}}$$

**Interpretation:** This extraordinarily high crossover temperature (~4906 °C) means magnetite formation remains thermodynamically spontaneous at every practically achievable temperature. Even if you heat iron to its boiling point (~3134 K), $\Delta G^\circ$ is still negative. This is consistent with the well-known observation that iron oxidises at essentially all accessible temperatures — preventing rust requires kinetic barriers (coatings, cathodic protection), not thermodynamic ones.

**Placement in the $\Delta H$–$\Delta S$ matrix (L3 §3.5):** This reaction sits in the lower-left cell — exothermic ($\Delta H < 0$) and entropy-decreasing ($\Delta S < 0$). Such reactions are spontaneous only at **low $T$** (when $|T\Delta S|$ is smaller than $|\Delta H|$). With $T^* \approx 5179$ K, "low $T$" encompasses essentially the entire temperature range of interest.
L3|medium.final_answer: (a) $\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = -2236.8$ kJ/mol; $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = -431.90$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$. (b) $\Delta G^\circ_{298} = -2108.1$ kJ/mol (strongly spontaneous). (c) $T^* \approx 5179$ K — the reaction remains spontaneous at all practical temperatures.
common_mistakes: **Forgetting to multiply by stoichiometric coefficients.** The reaction produces 2 mol Fe$_3$O$_4$ and consumes 4 mol Fe and 3 mol O$_2$. Students often apply $\Delta H_f^\circ$ and $S^\circ$ for one formula unit without multiplying, giving answers that are exactly half or some other fraction of the correct value.

**Using wrong units when combining $\Delta H$ and $T\Delta S$.** $\Delta H$ is typically in kJ/mol while $S^\circ$ values from tables are in J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$. Failing to convert $\Delta S$ to kJ mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ before computing $T\Delta S$ introduces a factor-of-1000 error in the entropy contribution, making $\Delta G$ appear incorrectly close to $\Delta H$.

**Setting $\Delta H_f^\circ = 0$ for O$_2$ but forgetting $S^\circ[\text{O}_2] \neq 0$.** Standard enthalpy of formation of elements in their standard state is zero, but standard molar entropy is NOT zero for any substance above 0 K (Third Law). Students sometimes omit the O$_2$ entropy contribution entirely when computing $\Delta S^\circ_{\text{rxn}}$, drastically underestimating the entropy decrease.
